lessons.culture: In the neighbourhood souk and at the local vegetable stall in Casablanca or Rabat, people ask the price with bshhal and a little polite bargaining is normal, though less so with a regular seller. lessons.culture: Almost every Moroccan neighbourhood has its own ferran (bakery or communal oven) and a butcher the family trusts, and khobz is bought fresh several times a day because it is eaten with every meal. Customers often ask the butcher to mince or cut the meat in front of them.

lessons.culture: Lunch is the main meal in a Moroccan home, and the family often eats from one shared dish, such as tajine or, on Fridays, couscous, scooping it up with bread. People say bismillah before eating, and afterwards al-7amdulillah is said and the cook is thanked with allah y3tik s-se77a. A host says bs-se77a w r-rah7a (to your health and comfort) to guests as they eat.

lessons.culture: Moroccans say they do not eat pork because they are Muslim, and the question is rarely asked outright when inviting a guest. If you dislike a host's dish, it is more polite to say al-7amdulillah, shb3t (thank God, I'm full) than to say ma kat3jebnish.

lessons.culture: In the old medinas of Casablanca and Rabat bargaining is expected: the seller names a high price and both sides meet in the middle, usually with a greeting and a smile first. Supermarkets and shops with printed prices do not bargain.
